html:
Chorrera was a culture of coastal and highland Ecuador from about 1300 to 300 BCE. It was one of the most widespread cultures of ancient Ecuador, reaching from the Pacific lowlands into the Andes and southern Colombia.

It grew out of earlier coastal traditions: Valdivia, one of the oldest pottery-making cultures in the Americas, and then Machalilla. Chorrera people lived in farming villages, growing maize, beans and root crops, and also fished and gathered shellfish.

They are best known for fine pottery:

  • thin, polished vessels, some painted with a shiny, iridescent finish;
  • whistling bottles, which make a sound when liquid or air moves inside;
  • hollow figurines of people.

Its styles spread widely and shaped the regional cultures that followed on the Ecuadorian coast. Chorrera was in its prime at the same time as Chavín in Peru and the Olmec in Mexico, though how much they were in touch is not clear.
sum: Chorrera was a culture of coastal and highland Ecuador from about 1300 to 300 BCE. It was one of the most widespread cultures of ancient Ecuador, reaching from the Pacific lowlands into the Andes and southern Colombia.
